reason_kind: change to the definition of correct
reasoning: The row was admitted on a narrow definition of done — one lenient branch closed so that a run naming an act on a no-act scenario fails — and a row closes against the DOD it was admitted on, not against what shipped. What shipped exceeds it: the same branch now also fails the extra-act case, which the eval's written cost model deliberately records as a note rather than a failure. That is a red check inside the accepted scope (four recorded runs flip red, 30 to 26, on runs whose every other field is right) and a delivered artifact contradicting a decision already on record, so the closing kernel's bar — no close while the accepted scope holds a red check — is not met, and the trusted-closure clause that no threshold or scoring rule may be invented after start that was not in the admitted DOD is squarely violated: the score the eval reports is being redefined by a change nobody admitted. The pipeline also owes the standing duty to say plainly when the delivered work conflicts with a standing decision, which the cost model is. This is not the ordinary case where a shown result closes without waiting for his eye: what a run must count as failing is the definition of correct for the eval itself, and that fork is open — he closed one branch and said nothing about its sibling, and the only artifact that speaks says note, not failure, so no command, test or read settles which behaviour the wider case should have. It is also not a redefinition he ordered himself, since he named only the narrow case. The class hunt applies but stops exactly here: the sibling of the fixed case is identified, and its class boundary is the kind that calls for his judgment. So the pipeline states the overshoot, notes that splitting the two cases apart is possible and cheap, puts the one product question to him, and holds the row open until he answers.
